<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
This comment is valuable where it uses the microdata, and it overreaches in its conclusions. The record-based output and time-tracking corrections are the most useful new evidence on the Halden pilot. The attrition finding, if it holds, is serious. But the headline claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" goes beyond the comment's own estimates. It also passes over the randomised evidence the comment itself cites.

## Arithmetic checks

- **Table 2:** all four rows reproduce.
  - 95.1 / 0.8 = 118.9
  - 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, and 98.4 / 0.859 = 114.6
  - 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861, and 95.4 / 0.861 = 110.8
- **Revenue:** 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, a real fall of about 2.6%.
- **Hours decomposition in §3 doesn't reconcile.** Thirty-two scheduled hours, plus 0.7 hours on each of four days, plus 1.6 hours on the day off, gives about 36.4 hours. Starting from baseline actual days (40.3 / 5 = 8.06 hours) gives about 36.6. The reported pilot average is 34.6.
  - Taking the 34.6 total and 1.6 hours on the day off as given, the four working days average about 8.25 hours.
  - That is roughly 0.2–0.25 hours longer than a scheduled or baseline day, not 0.7.
  - Either the +0.7 figure or the 34.6 total needs correcting. It doesn't change Table 2, which uses the totals, but it is the kind of error a critique like this can't afford.
- **Month-ten extrapolation (§6).** A linear decline from 0.61 at month three to 0.29 at month six reaches zero at about month 8.7, not month ten. Two points also don't establish that the decline is linear.

## 1. The abstract misdescribes Table 2

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems reduces the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only two of them: the output measure and the hours denominator. Attrition isn't corrected anywhere.

That could be fixed by bounding the attrition effect, for example with Lee-style bounds or by imputing low outcomes for the nine organisations that withdrew. Alternatively, the abstract should drop the claim.

## 2. The sequence in Table 2 mixes corrections with changes in sample

The four rows use different samples: 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The fall from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore combines two things:
- the effect of the corrections, and
- the effect of switching to a different, non-random subset.

The data note concedes this, but the abstract still headlines 23.4 → 10.8.

The clean version is a within-sample decomposition for the 17 organisations: their as-reported gain, then output corrected, then hours corrected, then both. If the 17 organisations' as-reported gain is close to 23.4%, the headline holds. If it isn't, part of the drop comes from sample composition, not measurement.

Confidence intervals are also missing. With 17 or 23 organisations, a 10.8% point estimate could carry a wide interval.

## 3. The record-based index is not a neutral benchmark

Among the record types listed is **"billable hours delivered."** That measures input, not output, and it falls mechanically when hours are cut. Any organisation whose records are billable hours will show an output fall roughly proportional to the hours cut, which biases the record-based index downward.

The comment should therefore:
- report how many of the 23 organisations used each record type, and
- recompute Table 1 excluding hours-based records.

The 19-of-23 pattern is strong evidence that the two measures diverge (a sign test gives p ≈ 0.003). How much of the 3.8-point gap reflects manager optimism, as opposed to records that track hours, is less clear.

## 4. Attrition: the most important new fact, under-analysed

The working paper says the withdrawals occurred "during the preparation phase." According to the microdata, seven of the nine came after the reduced schedule began, six of them for workload or output reasons. If so, the working paper misdescribed its own sample in a way that flatters the result.

That deserves:
- a direct statement of the discrepancy, ideally after checking with the Halden authors in case the microdata coding differs; and
- a quantitative bound. Do the withdrawn organisations have any output data from their first months? If so, an analysis including every enrolled organisation, which the comment itself recommends, may be partly possible.

## 5. Selective use of the Varden trial

The comment calls Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature" and uses it to support its conclusion. But the same trial cuts against the comment's main claim in two ways.

**Varden already applies the comment's corrections.** It uses record-based output, actual hours from timesheets, and a randomised control group, which covers most of what the comment recommends. It still finds **+12.5% output per actual hour** in case processing (CI +6.9 to +18.4).

**The counter stratum also shows a per-hour gain.** It found +6.7% per actual hour (CI +0.4 to +13.3), alongside the 11.4% fall in output per employee.

So the best-controlled evidence available shows per-hour gains that survive the corrections the comment proposes. Neither trial lasted long enough to exclude novelty, and Varden staff knew they were being evaluated. Those are fair reasons to doubt durability. They are not grounds for calling the gains "entirely an artifact." The comment should either engage with this result or narrow its claim.

## 6. Novelty: plausible, but not demonstrated

**Energy is not output.** The novelty argument rests on a decline in self-reported energy. A fading sense of energy doesn't show that productivity is fading.

**The comment has the data to test this directly.** The Halden index was collected monthly, and the comment has the microdata. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should decline from month to month, especially in the 17-organisation subset with records and actual hours. This is the single most useful analysis missing from the comment.

**"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter"** is a rhetorical position, not a finding. A residual gain of about 11% that the comment hasn't explained is a reason for uncertainty, not a reason to set the estimate to zero.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis is treated unfairly

**The characterisation is inaccurate.** The Varden authors labelled the analysis unregistered and exploratory, said explicitly that it "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test. The comment's statement that the offices were "selected for analysis after the results were known" isn't supported by the Varden text. The calendar data were collected in month six, before the nine-month results.

**There is independent corroboration.** The Halden pilot reports cuts to recurring meetings in 47 of 58 manager interviews. That is a different source and a different method, and it is qualitative, but it is not nothing.

**It competes directly with the novelty account.** If part of the gain comes from removing low-value meeting time, that is a structural change with no reason to fade. Under the comment's own framework, the meetings hypothesis is the main alternative to novelty and should be tested, not dismissed.

"Should not be cited as an established mechanism" is fair. "Should not be cited" is not.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Revenue.** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, which mostly depends on output prices in the relevant sectors. The direction of the correction is right, though, and this matches my earlier point about the nominal figure.
- **The retail evidence is thin.** The 11.2% retail figure rests on three organisations and should say so in the text.
- **The concluding sentence about presence-dependent work** is supported for output *per employee*. It shouldn't be read as evidence about output per hour, where Varden found a small gain.
- **The subsets may not be representative.** Organisations with time tracking and submitted records may be systematically better or worse managed. The data note acknowledges this, but nothing in the abstract or conclusion reflects it.

## Overall

The comment's corrections are a real contribution:
- managers' reports were systematically higher than the records,
- actual hours fell about 14%, not 20%, and
- the sample is survivors.

Together these probably halve the Halden estimate. On the evidence presented, the defensible conclusion is narrower than the one stated: *"The Halden pilot overstated the per-hour gain by at least half; a residual gain of roughly 10% remains in the correctable subset and is consistent with randomised evidence, though its durability is untested."*

The stronger claim, that the gains are "entirely an artifact," would require two things the comment doesn't provide: evidence that per-hour output declines over time, and an account of why the Varden per-hour gains should be dismissed.

Across all three documents, the picture is fairly consistent:
- Per-hour gains are real but much smaller than the pilot claimed, roughly 7–13% against actual hours.
- Per-employee output holds where work isn't tied to presence and falls where it is.
- Durability is the open question.

If useful, I can draft a referee report for the comment or a short synthesis note setting the three documents side by side.
